growth_story.headline: Namibia's commodity boom ended in 2016; income per person fell over the next decade, and a diamond slump keeps the recovery slow.
growth_story.arc: Namibia's income per person barely grew from 1990 to 2001, at 0.3 percent a year. From 2002 to 2015 it rose 3.3 percent a year, as a global commodity boom drew mining investment and public spending expanded quickly. Growth stopped in 2016 when the commodity cycle ended, big investment projects were completed, a severe drought hit and the government began tightening the budget to slow rising debt; income per person shrank every year from 2016 to 2019 and fell 10.7 percent in the 2020 pandemic. Demand for diamonds and uranium drove a partial recovery from 2021, but from 2016 to 2025 income per person averaged -1.6 percent a year. In 2025 it slipped 0.3 percent as the diamond slump deepened, leaving it 15.8 percent below its 2015 peak and about where it first stood in 2007.

threads.title: Commodity boom and spending surge
threads.text: From 2002 to 2015 income per person grew 3.3 percent a year. The World Bank links this to a global commodity boom that spurred mining investment and exports, together with a fast rise in public spending.

since_last_year.text: Growth stayed slow through 2025 and into early 2026 as diamond output kept falling, and income per person slipped 0.3 percent in 2025. A sharp drop in customs union revenue widened the budget deficit, while stronger uranium and gold exports narrowed the current account deficit. Foreign investment, concentrated in mining and energy, paid for most of that deficit, and the World Bank sees petroleum and green hydrogen as possible future gains.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe a recovery since 2021, with total output growing every year, but in the data income per person rose only 1.7 and 1.5 percent in 2023 and 2024 and fell 0.3 percent in 2025, as the population grew almost as fast as the economy. The World Bank expects job creation to "barely outpace population growth." It also cites notable gains in GDP per capita since independence, yet in 2025 income per person was about where it first stood in 2007.
